title: Python Files, Text & Regular Expressions
sub: Read and write files, parse CSV, JSON, dates and logs with re, and make Python behave in a shell pipeline
goals: Open, read, write and close files safely with with, in text and binary mode
Manipulate paths with pathlib and know when to reach for os, shutil and glob
Read and write CSV and JSON, and parse timestamps with datetime
Write regular expressions with groups, named groups, flags and lazy quantifiers, and apply them with re
Write a Python tool that reads stdin, writes stdout, reports errors on stderr and sets an exit status
Finish loganalyzer.py as a stdin-to-stdout command-line tool

blocks.text: Until now your Python programs lived inside themselves: the data was a string or a list in the source. Real tools read files, accept data from other programs and leave results where the next program can pick them up. This chapter connects Python to the outside world with the same model you learned in [Streams, redirection and pipes](#pipes): a program reads one stream, writes another, and reports problems separately. You will learn files, paths, CSV, JSON, dates and regular expressions, then turn `loganalyzer.py` into a command you can drop into a pipeline.

blocks.title: How the in-page examples handle files

blocks.text: The Python in this page runs in your browser, which has no access to your real files. Examples therefore use `io.StringIO`, an in-memory object that behaves exactly like an open file, and temporary directories that vanish when the block ends. The code is identical to what you write for real files; only the source of the data differs. Snippets that need your real machine are marked `python` or `file` and are meant for PyCharm and Terminal.
Files are streams

When you call `open()`, Python asks the operating system for a **file descriptor** (the small integer from the streams chapter), wraps it in a **file object**, and adds a **buffer**: a chunk of memory that batches reads and writes so the program does not make one system call per character.

blocks.code:
your code            Python file object                 kernel
  ┌─────────┐  write  ┌────────────────────────┐  write()  ┌──────────────┐
  │ f.write │ ──────▶ │ text layer  (encoding) │           │  fd 3        │ ──▶ disk
  │ ("GET") │         │ buffer (typ. 128 KiB)  │ ────────▶ │  file offset │
  └─────────┘         └────────────────────────┘  on flush └──────────────┘
                        ⟪c:flush⟫ or ⟪c:close⟫ sends the buffer down; a crash before then loses it

blocks.text: Three consequences follow. Data you wrote may not be on disk until the buffer is flushed or the file is closed. A file left open holds a descriptor, and every process has a limit on those. And text files have an **encoding** layer that converts between the characters in your program and the bytes on disk.

blocks.title: Why the file objects of stdin and stdout look the same

blocks.text: `sys.stdin`, `sys.stdout` and `sys.stderr` are file objects too, wrapped around descriptors 0, 1 and 2. Everything below about reading and writing applies to them unchanged, which is what makes Python a good citizen in a pipeline (see the end of this chapter).
open() and the with statement

blocks.name: open()
blocks.sum: Open a file and return a file object for reading or writing.
blocks.syntax: open(file, mode='r', encoding=None, errors=None, newline=None) -> file object

how.text: `mode` is a string of letters: `r` read (default), `w` write and truncate, `a` append, `x` create and fail if the file exists, `+` read and write, `t` text (default) and `b` binary. In text mode Python decodes bytes to `str` with `encoding`; if you leave it out, Python 3.15 uses UTF-8 but older versions (including the 3.13 in-page runner) use the machine's locale, so write `encoding="utf-8"` explicitly in anything you share. In binary mode you get `bytes` and no decoding happens.

Opening a file that does not exist for reading raises `FileNotFoundError`; opening somewhere you may not write raises `PermissionError`. Always use `open` inside a `with` block so the file is closed even if an error occurs.

examples.desc: Open, write, then read back in a temporary directory
examples.code:
import tempfile, os
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    path = os.path.join(d, "hosts.txt")
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("example.com\n")
        f.write("python.org\n")
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        print(f.read().splitlines())
    with open(path, "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("github.com\n")
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        print(f.read())

examples.desc: Python's read-and-filter loop is the same idea as grep
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; [print(l, end="") for l in open("access.log", encoding="utf-8") if " 404 " in l]' | head -3

anat.exp: mode: write, truncating the file first

gotchas: `"w"` empties an existing file the moment `open` returns, before you write anything. Use `"a"` to add, or `"x"` to refuse to overwrite.

blocks.name: with (Python)
blocks.sum: Run a block with a resource that is cleaned up automatically, even after an error.

how.text: `with` calls the object's `__enter__` method, gives you its result as `name`, runs the indented block, and always calls `__exit__` afterwards, whether the block finished normally, used `return`, or raised an exception. For files, `__exit__` flushes and closes. You can open several at once: `with open(a) as src, open(b, "w") as dst:`.

examples.desc: The file is closed when the block ends
examples.code:
import io
with io.StringIO("line one\nline two\n") as f:
    first = f.readline()
print(repr(first), f.closed)

blocks.text: Reading: four patterns

blocks.code:
import io
text = "alpha\nbeta\n\ngamma"

f = io.StringIO(text)
print(repr(f.read()))                  # 1. everything at once

f = io.StringIO(text)
print(f.readlines())                   # 2. a list of lines (newlines kept)

f = io.StringIO(text)
for line in f:                          # 3. iterate: one line at a time, lazily
    print(repr(line.rstrip("\n")))

f = io.StringIO(text)
print([ln.strip() for ln in f if ln.strip()])   # 4. iterate and filter blanks

blocks.title: Read a file line by line

tokens.exp: keyword: open the resource and guarantee cleanup
the call that returns a file object, decoding bytes as UTF-8
the name bound to the file object inside the block
the indented block follows; the file closes when it ends
the file object is an iterator: one line per pass, lazily
each line still carries its newline until you strip it

blocks.text: Use pattern 3 for anything large: the file object is its own iterator and reads one line at a time, so memory use stays constant for a ten-gigabyte log. `read()` and `readlines()` load everything, which is fine for a small config file and a mistake for a big one. Lines keep their trailing `\n`; `rstrip("\n")` or `strip()` removes it.

blocks.name: file.read()
blocks.sum: Read the rest of a file (or n characters) as one string.

how.text: Loads everything from the current position to the end into memory. Fine for config files, risky for a multi-gigabyte log; loop over the file object instead. Returns an empty string at end of file.

examples.code:
import io
f = io.StringIO('alpha
beta
gamma
')
print(repr(f.read(5)), repr(f.read()), repr(f.read()))

examples.desc: Read stdin completely and count its words
examples.code: seq 1 5 | python3 -c 'import sys; print(len(sys.stdin.read().split()))'

gotchas: After `read()` the position is at the end, so a second `read()` returns `''` until you `seek(0)`.

blocks.name: file.readline()
blocks.sum: Read one line, including its newline character.

how.text: Returns `''` at end of file, which is how a `while` loop knows to stop; a blank line in the file is `'\n'`, not `''`. Iterating with `for line in f` is the usual and faster way.

examples.code:
import io
f = io.StringIO('one\n\nthree')
print(repr(f.readline()), repr(f.readline()), repr(f.readline()), repr(f.readline()))

examples.desc: Peel off a header line, then process the rest
examples.code:
printf 'header
row1
row2
' | python3 -c 'import sys; print("skipped:", sys.stdin.readline().strip()); print(sys.stdin.read().upper(), end="")'

blocks.name: file.write()
blocks.sum: Write a string to a file and return the number of characters written.

how.text: Does not add a newline; you supply `'\n'`. Text is buffered, so data may not reach the disk until `flush()` or `close()`; the `with` statement closes for you. `print(..., file=f)` also writes and adds the newline.

examples.code:
import io
f = io.StringIO()
n = f.write('GET /\n')
print('HEAD /', file=f)
print(n, repr(f.getvalue()))

examples.desc: Write to stdout and let wc count the lines
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; sys.stdout.write("GET /\n"); print("HEAD /", file=sys.stdout)' | wc -l

blocks.name: file.seek()
blocks.sum: Move the read/write position inside a file.

how.text: `whence` 0 is from the start, 1 from the current position, 2 from the end. `tell()` reports the position. Text files only allow seeking to positions returned by `tell()` or to 0; binary files allow any offset.

examples.code:
import io
f = io.StringIO('abcdef')
f.read(3)
print(f.tell())
f.seek(0)
print(f.read(2), f.tell())

examples.desc: A pipe cannot seek, so rewinding needs a real file
examples.code: echo abc | python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.stdin.seekable())'

blocks.name: io.StringIO
blocks.sum: Create an in-memory text file.

how.text: Behaves like a file opened with `open()`: `read`, `readline`, `write`, iteration, `seek`. Nothing touches the disk, so it is the way to test file-reading code with a literal string. `getvalue()` returns everything written. `io.BytesIO` is the binary twin.

examples.code:
import io
src = io.StringIO('a,1\nb,2\n')
for line in src:
    print(line.rstrip().split(','))
out = io.StringIO()
out.write('done')
print(out.getvalue())

examples.desc: Feed a function from a pipe the same way as from a test string
examples.code: seq 3 | python3 -c 'import sys; print([int(l) * 2 for l in sys.stdin])'

gotchas: A function that takes a file object (not a filename) works with real files and StringIO alike. Design your parsers that way.

blocks.text: Writing

blocks.code:
import io
out = io.StringIO()
out.write("ip,hits\n")
for ip, n in [("10.0.0.5", 40), ("10.0.0.9", 7)]:
    print(f"{ip},{n}", file=out)         # print can write to any file object
out.writelines(["10.0.0.2,3\n", "10.0.0.7,1\n"])
print(out.getvalue(), end="")

blocks.text: `print(..., file=f)` is often nicer than `f.write` because it adds the newline and converts numbers. To append to a real file use mode `"a"`. To avoid leaving a half-written file if the program dies, write to a temporary name and rename it afterwards (`Path.replace`), which is atomic on the same volume.

blocks.code:
from pathlib import Path

report = Path("report.txt")
tmp = report.with_suffix(".tmp")
with open(tmp, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("finished\n")
tmp.replace(report)          # atomic swap: readers see the old file or the new one, never half

blocks.text: Text, bytes and encodings

A computer stores bytes; a `str` holds characters. An **encoding** is the rule that maps one to the other. **UTF-8** is the standard: ASCII characters take one byte, others take two to four. Mixing the two is the source of the classic `UnicodeDecodeError`.

blocks.code:
s = "naïve café"
b = s.encode("utf-8")
print(len(s), len(b))                    # 10 characters, 12 bytes
print(b)
print(b.decode("utf-8") == s)
print(ascii(b.decode("latin-1")))        # wrong codec: mojibake, no error
print(ascii(b.decode("ascii", errors="replace")))
try:
    b.decode("ascii")
except UnicodeDecodeError as err:
    print(type(err).__name__, "at byte", err.start)
blocks.out:
10 12
b'na\xc3\xafve caf\xc3\xa9'
True
'na\xc3\xafve caf\xc3\xa9'
'na\ufffd\ufffdve caf\ufffd\ufffd'
UnicodeDecodeError at byte 2

blocks.text: `errors="replace"` substitutes a placeholder for undecodable bytes, `errors="ignore"` drops them, and `errors="backslashreplace"` shows them as escapes. For a log from the wild, `open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")` keeps one bad byte from killing the whole run. Use binary mode (`"rb"`) when the file is not text at all, such as an image, a pcap, or a `struct`-packed header ([Computers](#computers)).

In text mode Python converts line endings: `
` on input becomes `
`, and `
` on output becomes the platform's ending. For the `csv` module open files with `newline=""` so it can manage endings itself, as shown in the cards below.
Paths

A path is a string until you ask the file system about it. `pathlib` wraps it in an object so that joining, splitting and testing become methods instead of string slicing. Python has older modules for the same jobs, and you will see them in existing code:

blocks.name: pathlib.Path
blocks.sum: Represent a file-system path as an object with methods.

how.text: Replaces string juggling with `os.path`. The `/` operator joins parts, and properties split them: `name`, `stem`, `suffix`, `suffixes`, `parent`, `parts`. `Path.home()` and `Path.cwd()` give the common starting points. Creating a `Path` touches nothing; methods like `exists()` ask the file system. `PurePosixPath` does only string work, with no file system access.

examples.code:
from pathlib import PurePosixPath
p = PurePosixPath('/Users/me/lab') / 'data' / 'report-2026-09.csv.gz'
print(p.name, p.stem, p.suffix, p.suffixes)
print(p.parent, p.parts[-2:], p.with_suffix('.txt').name)
print(p.is_absolute(), PurePosixPath('a/../b').as_posix())

examples.desc: Print the extension of each argument from the shell
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; from pathlib import Path; print(*(Path(a).suffix for a in sys.argv[1:]))' a.txt b.tar.gz

blocks.name: Path.read_text()
blocks.sum: Read a whole file as text in one call.

how.text: Opens, reads and closes the file for you. Pass `encoding='utf-8'` explicitly so behaviour does not depend on the Python version or, before 3.15, the machine's locale. `read_bytes()` is the binary twin. Use it for small files; loop over `open()` for large ones.

examples.code:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    p = Path(d) / 'hosts.txt'
    p.write_text('example.com\npython.org\n', encoding='utf-8')
    print(p.read_text(encoding='utf-8').splitlines())

examples.desc: Read the file named by the previous command
examples.code: echo /etc/hosts | python3 -c 'import sys; from pathlib import Path; print(len(Path(sys.stdin.read().strip()).read_text().splitlines()), "lines")'

blocks.name: Path.write_text()
blocks.sum: Write a string to a file, replacing its contents.

how.text: Creates the file if needed and overwrites it otherwise, returning the number of characters written. For appending use `open(path, 'a')`.

examples.code:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    p = Path(d, 'notes.txt')
    print(p.write_text('first\n'), p.write_text('second\n'))
    print(p.read_text())

examples.desc: Save what arrives on stdin, like tee, then check it
examples.code: seq 3 | python3 -c 'import sys; from pathlib import Path; Path("notes.txt").write_text(sys.stdin.read())' && cat notes.txt

gotchas: It truncates without asking, like shell `>`.

blocks.name: Path.glob()
blocks.sum: Yield the paths that match a glob pattern, optionally searching subfolders.

how.text: `glob('*.log')` matches in one folder; `rglob('*.log')` searches below it as well (it is the recursive form of `glob`). The patterns use shell wildcards `* ? [ab]`. The result is a generator in arbitrary order, so wrap it in `sorted()`. Unlike the shell, an unmatched pattern yields nothing instead of an error.

examples.code:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    root = Path(d)
    (root / 'archive').mkdir()
    for name in ['a.log', 'b.log', 'c.txt', 'archive/old.log']:
        (root / name).write_text('x')
    print(sorted(p.name for p in root.glob('*.log')))
    print(sorted(str(p.relative_to(root)) for p in root.rglob('*.log')))
find . -name '*.log'

blocks.name: Path.mkdir()
blocks.sum: Create a directory, optionally with missing parents.

how.text: `parents=True` is `mkdir -p`: it creates every missing level. `exist_ok=True` suppresses the error when the folder already exists. Without it, an existing folder raises `FileExistsError`.

examples.code:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    target = Path(d) / 'a' / 'b' / 'c'
    target.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    target.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    print(target.is_dir(), target.exists(), (target / 'x').exists())

examples.desc: Create one directory tree per input line
examples.code: printf 'logs/2026\nlogs/2027\n' | python3 -c 'import sys; from pathlib import Path; [Path(l.strip()).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) for l in sys.stdin]' && ls logs

blocks.text: A real-world snippet for Terminal: list the five biggest files under a folder, the Python version of `find ... | xargs ls -lS | head`.

blocks.code:
from pathlib import Path

root = Path.home() / "lab"
files = [p for p in root.rglob("*") if p.is_file()]
for p in sorted(files, key=lambda p: p.stat().st_size, reverse=True)[:5]:
    print(f"{p.stat().st_size:>8}  {p.relative_to(root)}")

blocks.title: shutil.rmtree and Path.unlink have no undo

blocks.text: They delete immediately, with no Trash. Print what you would delete first, test with a folder of copies, and never build a path to delete from unchecked user input.
CSV

**CSV** (comma-separated values) looks easy and is not: fields can contain commas inside quotes, quotes inside quotes, and even line breaks. `line.split(",")` breaks on those. The `csv` module implements the rules. It takes any iterable of lines, so it works the same on a file or a `StringIO`.

blocks.name: csv.reader()
blocks.sum: Iterate over the rows of a CSV file as lists of strings.

how.text: Takes any iterable of lines, usually a file opened with `newline=''`. It handles quoted fields that contain commas or newlines, which `line.split(',')` gets wrong. Every value is a string, so convert numbers yourself.

examples.code:
import csv, io
data = io.StringIO('name,role\nalice,admin\n"smith, bob",dev\n')
rows = list(csv.reader(data))
print(rows)
print(rows[2][0], 'a,b'.split(','))

examples.desc: Compare with the shell, which splits on every comma
examples.code: python3 -c 'import csv, sys; print(len(next(csv.reader(sys.stdin))))' < users.csv

gotchas: Open real files with `newline=''` so the csv module controls line endings.

blocks.name: csv.DictReader()
blocks.sum: Read CSV rows as dicts keyed by the header row.

how.text: The first row becomes the keys, so you write `row['ip']` instead of `row[2]` and the code survives column reordering. Missing fields become `None`, extras are collected under the key `None`. In Python 3.8 and later each row is a plain `dict`.

examples.code:
import csv, io
data = io.StringIO('name,role,ip,port\nalice,admin,10.0.0.5,22\nbob,dev,10.0.0.12,8080\n')
for row in csv.DictReader(data):
    print(row['name'], row['ip'], int(row['port']) < 1024)
python3 -c 'import csv, sys; print(sum(r["role"] == "admin" for r in csv.DictReader(sys.stdin)))' < users.csv

blocks.name: csv.writer()
blocks.sum: Write rows of values as CSV, quoting where needed.

how.text: `writerow` takes one sequence and `writerows` takes many. Values containing commas, quotes or newlines are quoted automatically. Numbers are converted with `str()`. On disk, open with `newline=''`.

examples.code:
import csv, io
out = io.StringIO()
w = csv.writer(out, lineterminator='\n')
w.writerow(['ip', 'hits'])
w.writerows([['10.0.0.5', 40], ['smith, bob', 2]])
print(out.getvalue(), end='')

examples.desc: Hand CSV to sort, ordered by the hits column
examples.code: python3 -c 'import csv, sys; csv.writer(sys.stdout, lineterminator="\n").writerows([["10.0.0.5", 40], ["10.0.0.9", 7]])' | sort -t, -k2 -n

blocks.name: csv.DictWriter()
blocks.sum: Write dicts as CSV rows under a fixed header.

how.text: `fieldnames` fixes the column order. Call `writeheader()` once, then `writerow(dict)`. A key not in `fieldnames` raises `ValueError` unless you pass `extrasaction='ignore'`.

examples.code:
import csv, io
out = io.StringIO()
w = csv.DictWriter(out, fieldnames=['ip', 'hits'], lineterminator='\n')
w.writeheader()
w.writerow({'ip': '10.0.0.5', 'hits': 40})
print(out.getvalue(), end='')

examples.desc: Turn whitespace-separated text into CSV with a header
examples.code:
printf '10.0.0.5 40
10.0.0.9 7
' | python3 -c 'import csv, sys; w = csv.DictWriter(sys.stdout, fieldnames=["ip", "hits"], lineterminator="
"); w.writeheader(); [w.writerow(dict(zip(["ip", "hits"], l.split()))) for l in sys.stdin]'

tokens.exp: open for text reading; newline="" lets csv handle line endings
first row becomes the field names
one dict per remaining row
look a column up by name instead of position
every value is a string until you convert it

blocks.code:
import csv, io
users = io.StringIO("""name,role,ip,port
alice,admin,10.0.0.5,22
bob,dev,10.0.0.12,8080
carol,dev,192.168.1.50,22
""")
rows = list(csv.DictReader(users))
print(rows[0])
ssh = [r["name"] for r in rows if r["port"] == "22"]
print(ssh)
by_role = {}
for r in rows:
    by_role.setdefault(r["role"], []).append(r["name"])
print(by_role)

blocks.text: With a real file the shape is `with open("users.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f: for row in csv.DictReader(f): ...`. Remember every value is a string: `"22"` is not `22`.
JSON
**JSON** is the lingua franca of APIs and config files, and it maps directly onto lists, dicts, strings, numbers, booleans and `None`.

blocks.name: json.loads()
blocks.sum: Parse a JSON string into Python objects.

how.text: Objects become dicts, arrays lists, strings `str`, numbers `int` or `float`, and `true`, `false`, `null` become `True`, `False`, `None`. Invalid text raises `json.JSONDecodeError` (a `ValueError`) with the line and column. `json.load(f)` does the same from an open file.

examples.code:
import json
doc = json.loads('{"ip": "10.0.0.5", "ports": [22, 80], "up": true, "note": null}')
print(doc['ports'][1], doc['up'], doc['note'])
try:
    json.loads('{bad json}')
except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
    print('error at column', e.colno)
echo '{"a": [1, 2]}' | python3 -m json.tool

gotchas: JSON needs double quotes and has no trailing commas, which is stricter than a Python literal.

blocks.name: json.dumps()
blocks.sum: Convert Python objects to a JSON string.

how.text: `indent=2` pretty-prints, `sort_keys=True` makes output stable for diffs, `separators=(',', ':')` is compact, and `ensure_ascii=False` keeps non-ASCII characters readable. Dict keys become strings. Types JSON lacks, such as `set` and `datetime`, raise `TypeError` unless `default=str` (or a function) converts them. `json.dump(obj, f)` writes to a file.

examples.code:
import json
data = {'top': [['10.0.0.5', 40]], 'bad': 2, 'tags': {'b', 'a'}}
print(json.dumps({'ip': '10.0.0.5', 'n': 2}, sort_keys=True))
print(json.dumps(data, default=sorted, indent=2))

examples.desc: Format a Counter result for another program
examples.code: python3 -c 'import json; print(json.dumps({"requests": 120}, indent=2))' | jq .requests

gotchas: Tuples come back from `loads` as lists, and integer dict keys come back as strings.

blocks.name: json.dump()
blocks.sum: Write Python objects as JSON to an open file; json.load reads them back.

how.text: The file-object versions of `dumps` and `loads`. Open the file in text mode with `encoding='utf-8'`. For logs with one record per line (**JSON Lines**), write one `json.dumps(obj)` per line instead of one big document, so a crash never corrupts earlier records.

examples.code:
import json, io
buf = io.StringIO()
json.dump({'hosts': ['gw', 'nas']}, buf)
buf.seek(0)
print(json.load(buf)['hosts'])

examples.desc: Write JSON to stdout and read it back from a pipe with json.load
examples.code: python3 -c 'import json, sys; json.dump({"hosts": ["gw", "nas"]}, sys.stdout)' | python3 -c 'import json, sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["hosts"])'

blocks.code:
import json
records = [{"ip": "10.0.0.5", "hits": 40, "paths": ["/", "/login"]}, {"ip": "10.0.0.9", "hits": 7, "paths": []}]
text = json.dumps(records, indent=2, sort_keys=True)
print(text)
back = json.loads(text)
print(back == records, type(back[0]["hits"]))
print(json.dumps({"compact": [1, 2]}, separators=(",", ":")))

blocks.text: Two details bite. JSON has no tuples or sets, so `dumps` turns a tuple into a list and refuses a set unless you pass `default=`. And JSON object keys are always strings, so `{1: "a"}` round-trips as `{"1": "a"}`.
Dates and times

Log files carry timestamps as text. The `datetime` module parses them into objects you can compare, subtract and reformat. A datetime is **aware** when it knows its UTC offset and **naive** when it does not; mixing the two in arithmetic raises `TypeError`. When in doubt, parse with the offset (`%z`) and convert to UTC.

blocks.name: datetime.strptime()
blocks.sum: Parse a string into a datetime using a format.

how.text: Each `%` code names a field: `%d` day, `%b` abbreviated month name, `%Y` four-digit year, `%H:%M:%S` time, `%z` UTC offset such as `+0000`. Raises `ValueError` when the text does not fit. Month names follow the current locale, so `%b` may fail on a non-English system.

examples.code:
from datetime import datetime
t = datetime.strptime('07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000', '%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z')
print(t, t.hour, t.weekday(), t.isoformat())

examples.desc: Normalise log timestamps from a pipe to ISO form
examples.code: printf '07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000\n' | python3 -c 'import sys; from datetime import datetime; [print(datetime.strptime(l.strip(), "%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z").isoformat()) for l in sys.stdin]'

gotchas: Without `%z` you get a naive datetime that has no time zone; subtracting naive from aware raises `TypeError`.

blocks.name: datetime.strftime()
blocks.sum: Format a datetime as text.

how.text: The inverse of `strptime`, using the same codes. `isoformat()` is the unambiguous standard (`2026-10-07T09:14:08+00:00`). Use `strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M')` to build a per-minute bucket key for a log.

examples.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
t = datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 14, 8, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
print(t.strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M'), t.strftime('%a %d %b'), t.isoformat())

examples.desc: Format the epoch seconds printed by date
examples.code: date +%s | python3 -c 'import sys; from datetime import datetime; print(datetime.fromtimestamp(int(sys.stdin.read())).strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"))'

blocks.name: timedelta
blocks.sum: Represent a span of time, usable in date arithmetic.

how.text: Subtracting two datetimes gives a `timedelta`; adding one to a datetime gives a datetime. `total_seconds()` converts to a float, which is what you want for rates and thresholds. `.days` and `.seconds` are components, not totals.

examples.code:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
a = datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 14, 8)
b = datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 31, 2)
gap = b - a
print(gap, gap.total_seconds(), a + timedelta(hours=36))

examples.desc: Subtract two timestamps arriving as lines
examples.code: printf '09:14:08\n09:31:02\n' | python3 -c 'import sys; from datetime import datetime as d; a, b = [d.strptime(l.strip(), "%H:%M:%S") for l in sys.stdin]; print((b - a).total_seconds())'

tokens.exp: the text from the log
day of the month, two digits (07)
abbreviated month name between slashes (Oct)
four-digit year (2026)
hour, minute, second
UTC offset as +HHMM (+0000)

blocks.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta

FMT = "%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z"
first = datetime.strptime("07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000", FMT)
last = datetime.strptime("07/Oct/2026:09:52:42 +0000", FMT)
span = last - first
print(span, round(span.total_seconds() / 60, 1), "minutes")

local = datetime.strptime("07/Oct/2026:05:14:08 -0400", FMT)
print(local.astimezone(timezone.utc).isoformat(), local == first)

bucket = first.replace(second=0, microsecond=0)
print(bucket.strftime("%H:%M"), (bucket + timedelta(minutes=5)).strftime("%H:%M"))
print(datetime.fromisoformat("2026-10-07T09:14:08+00:00") == first)

blocks.text: `replace(second=0)` rounds a time down to the minute, the standard trick for "requests per minute" tables. `fromisoformat` parses the ISO form that `isoformat()` writes. The current time is `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`; avoid it in code you want to test, because the answer changes every run.
Regular expressions with re

A **regular expression** (regex) describes a pattern of text. You met the idea in `grep` and `sed` ([Text processing](#text)). Python's `re` module uses the Perl-style dialect (the one `grep -P` would give you, but not macOS's `grep`), which supports lazy quantifiers, named groups and lookahead. Start every pattern with the letter `r` (a **raw string**) so Python does not interpret backslashes before the regex engine sees them.

head: Syntax
Meaning
Example matches
rows: a set, a negated set, a range
start and end of the string (of each line with `re.M`)
zero or more, one or more, zero or one (greedy)
exactly n, between n and m
the lazy versions: match as little as possible
a group that does not capture
lookahead: followed by / not followed by, consumes nothing
escape a metacharacter to match it literally

blocks.code:
import re
line = '45.33.32.156 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000] "GET /api/v1/orders HTTP/1.1" 404 782'
print(re.search(r"\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+", line).group())     # first IPv4-looking text
m = re.search(r"\[(.*?)\]", line)                          # lazy: stop at the first ]
print(m.group(1))
m = re.search(r'"(\w+) (\S+) [^"]*" (\d{3}) (\d+)', line)
method, path, status, size = m.groups()
print(method, path, status, size)

blocks.text: Greedy against lazy

Quantifiers are **greedy** by default: they take as much as they can, then give back characters until the rest of the pattern fits. Add `?` to make them **lazy**: take as little as possible. This is the cause of most "my regex matched too much" bugs.

blocks.code: import re html = 'bold and italic' print(re.findall(r"<.+>", html)) # greedy: one long match from the first < to the last > print(re.findall(r"<.+?>", html)) # lazy: each tag separately print(re.findall(r"<[^>]+>", html)) # clearer still: "anything except >" q = 'say "one" then "two"' print(re.search(r'".*"', q).group(), re.search(r'".*?"', q).group(), re.findall(r'"([^"]*)"', q))

blocks.text: `[^"]*` ("anything except a quote") is faster and more predictable than `.*?`, and it cannot run past the closing delimiter. Use lazy quantifiers when the stop condition is more than one character.
Groups, named groups and match objects

Parentheses capture the text they match. `m.group(1)` is the first group, `m.groups()` is a tuple of all of them, and a **named group** `(?P<name>...)` can be read as `m["name"]` or all at once with `m.groupdict()`. Named groups document the pattern and survive edits that renumber the groups.

blocks.title: A named-group pattern for one log line

tokens.exp: raw string: backslashes reach the regex engine untouched
anchor: the match must start at the beginning of the line
named group "ip": one or more non-space characters
one or more whitespace characters
a literal [ then group "time": everything except ] then a literal ]
a literal quote, then group "method": capital letters
group "status": exactly three digits

blocks.code:
import re
pat = re.compile(r'^(?P<ip>\S+) \S+ \S+ \[(?P<time>[^\]]+)\] "(?P<method>[A-Z]+) (?P<path>\S+) [^"]*" (?P<status>\d{3}) (?P<bytes>\d+)')
line = '198.51.100.8 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:15:40 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 5120 "-" "Googlebot/2.1"'
m = pat.match(line)
print(m.groupdict())
print(m["status"], int(m["bytes"]) / 1024, m.start("path"), m.span("path"))
print(pat.match("not a log line"))

blocks.text: Flags and verbose mode

Flags change how a pattern behaves. Pass them as the last argument or inline: `re.I` / `re.IGNORECASE` (ignore case), `re.M` (`^` and `$` match at each line), `re.S` (`.` matches newline too), `re.X` / `re.VERBOSE` (ignore whitespace and allow `#` comments in the pattern).

blocks.code:
import re
text = "ERROR disk full\ninfo ok\nerror net down\n"
print(re.findall(r"^error.*$", text))                       # no flags: only lines starting lowercase 'error'
print(re.findall(r"^error.*$", text, re.I | re.M))          # ignore case, ^ and $ per line
print(re.findall(r"a.b", "a\nb"), re.findall(r"a.b", "a\nb", re.S))

IPV4 = re.compile(r"""
    \b
    (?:\d{1,3}\.){3}    # three octets, each followed by a dot
    \d{1,3}             # the last octet
    \b
""", re.VERBOSE)
print(IPV4.findall("gw 192.168.1.1, bad 1.2.3, dns 8.8.8.8"))

blocks.text: Verbose mode is how you keep a long pattern readable. Inside it a literal space must be written `\ ` or `[ ]`, and `#` starts a comment unless escaped.
Substitution and splitting
`re.sub` replaces matches; the replacement may refer to groups (`\1`, `\g<name>`) or be a function that receives each match. `re.split` splits on a pattern.

blocks.code:
import re
log = "src=192.168.1.23 dst=93.184.216.34 bytes=1500"
print(re.sub(r"(\d+)\.(\d+)\.(\d+)\.\d+", r"\1.\2.\3.x", log))
print(re.sub(r"bytes=(\d+)", lambda m: f"kb={int(m[1]) / 1000:.1f}", log))
print(re.sub(r"(?P<k>\w+)=(?P<v>\S+)", r"\g<v>:\g<k>", log))
print(re.split(r"\s+", "a  b\tc\nd"), re.split(r"[:/]", "10:20/30"))
print(re.subn(r"\d", "#", "a1b22"))

blocks.name: re.search()
blocks.sum: Find the first place a pattern matches anywhere in a string.

how.text: Scans left to right and returns a `Match` object for the first hit, or `None`. Always test the result before using it: `m = re.search(...)`, then `if m:`. `m.group(0)` is the whole match, `m.group(1)` the first group, `m.start()` and `m.end()` the position.

examples.code:
import re
m = re.search(r'time=([0-9.]+) ms', '64 bytes from 1.1.1.1: icmp_seq=0 ttl=58 time=11.842 ms')
print(m.group(0), '|', m.group(1), '|', m.span())
print(re.search(r'\d+', 'no digits'))
ping -c 3 localhost | grep -Eo 'time=[0-9.]+'

gotchas: Calling `.group()` on `None` raises `AttributeError`. This is the most common regex bug.

blocks.name: re.match()
blocks.sum: Match a pattern only at the start of a string.

how.text: Like `search`, but anchored at position 0 (not at the end). It is the check for "does this line start with the pattern". `re.fullmatch` demands the whole string match.

examples.code:
import re
print(bool(re.match(r'GET ', 'GET /')), bool(re.match(r'GET ', 'say GET')))
print(bool(re.match(r'\d+$', '123abc')), bool(re.fullmatch(r'\d+', '123abc')))

examples.desc: Keep only lines that start with a pattern, like grep with ^
examples.code:
printf 'GET /
say GET
GET /x
' | python3 -c 'import re, sys; [print(l, end="") for l in sys.stdin if re.match(r"GET ", l)]'

blocks.name: re.fullmatch()
blocks.sum: Match a pattern against the entire string.

how.text: Succeeds only if the pattern consumes every character, so it is the right tool for validation. It saves you from forgetting the `^` and `$` anchors.

examples.desc: Keep only valid port numbers, like grep -x
examples.code:
printf '22
8080
80a

' | python3 -c 'import re, sys; [print(l.strip()) for l in sys.stdin if re.fullmatch(r"\d{1,5}", l.strip())]'

blocks.name: re.findall()
blocks.sum: Return all non-overlapping matches as a list.

how.text: With no groups the list holds the matched strings. With one group it holds that group's text. With several groups it holds **tuples** of the groups. If you need positions or named groups, use `finditer`.

examples.code:
import re
text = 'gw 192.168.1.1, nas 192.168.1.20, bad 999.1.1'
print(re.findall(r'\b(?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}\b', text))
print(re.findall(r'(\w+) (\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', text))

examples.desc: Extract IPv4-looking strings from any text on stdin
examples.code: python3 -c 'import re, sys; print(*re.findall(r"\b(?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}\b", sys.stdin.read()), sep="\n")' < notes.txt

gotchas: The pattern `\d{1,3}` accepts 999. A regex checks shape, not meaning; validate octets with `ipaddress.ip_address()`.

blocks.name: re.finditer()
blocks.sum: Iterate over all matches as Match objects.

how.text: Lazily yields a `Match` for each hit, so you get positions (`m.start()`), named groups (`m.groupdict()`) and constant memory on large inputs.

examples.desc: Walk the key=value pairs of any text on stdin
examples.code: echo 'ttl=56 time=11 proto=icmp' | python3 -c 'import re, sys; [print(m["key"], m["val"]) for m in re.finditer(r"(?P<key>\w+)=(?P<val>\w+)", sys.stdin.read())]'

blocks.name: re.sub()
blocks.sum: Replace matches with a string, or with the result of a function.
blocks.syntax: re.sub(pattern, repl, string, count=0, flags=0) -> str

how.text: `repl` can use `\1` or `\g<name>` to reuse groups, or be a function that receives each `Match` and returns the replacement text. Returns a new string; the original is unchanged. `re.subn` also returns the number of replacements.

examples.code:
import re
line = 'src=192.168.1.23 dst=93.184.216.34'
print(re.sub(r'(\d+)\.(\d+)\.(\d+)\.(\d+)', r'\1.\2.\3.x', line))
print(re.sub(r'\d+', lambda m: str(int(m.group()) * 2), 'a1 b22'))

examples.desc: Mask the last octet of every address in a file
examples.code: python3 -c 'import re, sys; print(re.sub(r"(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)\.\d+", r"\1.x", sys.stdin.read()), end="")' < ips.txt | head -3

gotchas: Replacement strings treat backslashes specially. Use a raw string, `r'\1'`.

blocks.name: re.split()
blocks.sum: Split a string wherever a pattern matches.

how.text: More flexible than `str.split`: the separator can be any pattern, such as runs of mixed delimiters. If the pattern contains a capturing group, the separators are included in the result.

examples.code:
import re
print(re.split(r'[,;\s]+', 'a, b;c   d'))
print(re.split(r'(-)', 'a-b-c'), re.split(r'\s+', '  lead trail  '))

examples.desc: Turn mixed delimiters into one item per line and count them
examples.code: echo 'a, b;c   d' | python3 -c 'import re, sys; print("\n".join(re.split(r"[,;\s]+", sys.stdin.read().strip())))' | wc -l

gotchas: Leading or trailing separators produce empty strings at the ends.

blocks.name: re.compile()
blocks.sum: Compile a pattern once into a reusable object.

how.text: The compiled object has the same methods (`search`, `match`, `findall`, `finditer`, `sub`, `split`) without the pattern argument. Compile at module level for patterns used in a loop, and to attach flags and `re.VERBOSE` comments to a complex expression.

examples.code:
import re
PORT = re.compile(r':(\d+)$')
for target in ['10.0.0.5:22', '10.0.0.6', 'pi:8080']:
    m = PORT.search(target)
    print(target, '->', m.group(1) if m else None)

examples.desc: Compile once, then reuse the pattern on every input line
examples.code:
printf '10.0.0.5:22
10.0.0.6
pi:8080
' | python3 -c 'import re, sys; PORT = re.compile(r":(\d+)$"); [print(m.group(1)) for m in map(PORT.search, (l.strip() for l in sys.stdin)) if m]'

head: Mistake
Result
Fix
rows: Python warns about an invalid escape, and `"\b"` becomes a backspace character
finds nothing unless the pattern is at the start

blocks.text: The regex finds the right *shape*; the `ipaddress` module then checks the *values*. Combining a cheap shape test with a precise validator is a good habit for any network data.
A good citizen in the shell
A command that works in pipelines follows five habits, the same ones `grep` and `sort` follow:

items.text: **Read stdin** when no file is named, line by line, so it works on any amount of data.
**Write results to stdout** and nothing else, so the next command receives clean data.
**Write errors and progress to stderr** (`print(..., file=sys.stderr)`), so they reach you without polluting the pipe.
**Return an exit status**: 0 for success, non-zero for failure, via `sys.exit(n)`. The shell, `&&` and `if` read it from `$?`.
**Start with a shebang** and be executable, so it runs like any other command.

blocks.name: sys.stdin
blocks.sum: The standard input stream, a file-like object you can iterate over.

how.text: Connected to the keyboard or, in a pipeline, to the previous command's stdout. Iterating yields one line at a time with constant memory, so a script can process a log of any size. `read()` slurps everything and `readline()` returns one line. `input()` also reads from it but strips the newline and is meant for prompts.

examples.desc: Count non-blank lines of a file through a Python filter
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; print(sum(1 for l in sys.stdin if l.strip()))' < notes.txt

blocks.name: sys.exit()
blocks.sum: End the program with an exit status for the shell.

how.text: `sys.exit(0)` means success, any non-zero number means failure, and `sys.exit('message')` prints the message to stderr and exits with 1. It works by raising `SystemExit`, so `finally` blocks run. The shell sees the number in `$?`, so `&&`, `||` and `if` can react to your script.

examples.desc: Test a script's status from zsh
examples.code: python3 -c 'import sys; sys.exit(3)'; echo $?

blocks.text: Here is the smallest useful filter. Create `top.py` and run it with the Lab Kit data:

blocks.code:
cd ~/lab
chmod +x top.py
cat access.log | python3 top.py | sort -rn | head -3
./top.py < access.log | head -3
./top.py < /dev/null; echo "status $?"

$ cat access.log | python3 top.py | sort -rn | head -3
23 45.33.32.156
18 185.220.101.4
15 203.0.113.7
$ ./top.py < /dev/null; echo "status $?"
top.py: no input
status 1

blocks.text: `#!/usr/bin/env python3` finds `python3` on your `PATH`, which in a virtual environment is the right interpreter. `chmod +x` lets you run `./top.py` directly. The `sort -rn` is redundant because `most_common()` already sorts, but it shows that the output is plain text any tool can consume, which is the point.

`./top.py < huge.log | head -3` makes `head` exit after three lines. The next time Python writes to the closed pipe the write fails (Python ignores `SIGPIPE` by default, so the kernel's `EPIPE` error surfaces) and it prints a `BrokenPipeError` traceback. For a script meant for pipelines, add `import signal` and `signal.signal(signal.SIGPIPE, signal.SIG_DFL)` near the top (Unix only), which restores the quiet default behaviour shell tools have. `loganalyzer.py` below does this.
Running other programs: subprocess

Python can also drive the commands from the earlier chapters. `subprocess.run` starts a program, waits, and hands back its output and exit status. This needs a real machine, so these are `python` blocks for PyCharm.

blocks.code:
import subprocess

# Run a command, capture stdout and stderr as text, fail loudly on a non-zero status
result = subprocess.run(
    ["ping", "-c", "3", "-t", "10", "192.168.1.1"],
    capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=15,
)
print(result.returncode)
for line in result.stdout.splitlines():
    if "round-trip" in line:
        print(line.split("=")[1].split("/")[1], "ms average")

# check=True raises CalledProcessError for a non-zero exit status
# (dig exits 0 even for a name that does not exist; it fails when no server answers)
try:
    subprocess.run(["dig", "+short", "no-such-host.invalid"], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True, timeout=10)
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as err:
    print("dig failed with", err.returncode)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    print("dig timed out")

# A pipeline: ps aux | grep python, without involving a shell
ps = subprocess.Popen(["ps", "aux"], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
grep = subprocess.run(["grep", "python"], stdin=ps.stdout, capture_output=True, text=True)
ps.stdout.close()
print(len(grep.stdout.splitlines()), "python processes")

blocks.name: subprocess.run()
blocks.sum: Run another program, wait for it to finish and collect its result.
blocks.syntax: subprocess.run(args, *, capture_output=False, text=False, check=False, timeout=None, cwd=None, input=None) -> CompletedProcess

how.text: `args` is a **list** (`["dig", "+short", host]`), and the program is started directly without a shell, so spaces, quotes and special characters in a value are passed through exactly and cannot be interpreted as commands. `capture_output=True` collects stdout and stderr, `text=True` decodes them to `str`, `check=True` raises `CalledProcessError` on a non-zero status, and `timeout` raises `TimeoutExpired` and kills the child. The result has `.returncode`, `.stdout` and `.stderr`.
`shell=True` runs the string through `/bin/sh`, which allows pipes and globs but turns any untrusted text in the string into a command injection hole. Prefer a list and do the piping in Python.

examples.desc: Capture the output of a command from Python
examples.code: python3 -c 'import subprocess; r = subprocess.run(["uname", "-s"], capture_output=True, text=True); print(r.stdout.strip(), r.returncode)'

examples.desc: Show only the exit status of a command run from Python
examples.code: python3 -c 'import subprocess, sys; sys.exit(subprocess.run(["false"]).returncode)'; echo $?

gotchas: Never build the command with an f-string plus `shell=True` when any part comes from outside your program. `subprocess.run(f"ping {host}", shell=True)` with `host = "x; rm -rf ~"` is a disaster.

blocks.text: A list of arguments cannot be tricked into running extra commands. A single string with `shell=True` can. If you scan hosts from a file or an argument, pass them as list items.
Logging and argument parsing, a first look

Two standard-library modules turn a script into a tool. `logging` replaces scattered `print` calls with levelled messages sent to stderr, so you can turn the detail up or down without editing code. `argparse` builds the command-line interface (options, help text, error messages and exit status 2 for misuse).

blocks.name: logging.basicConfig()
blocks.sum: Set up simple logging for a script.

how.text: Call it once, early. Messages at or above `level` are written to stderr by default (stderr keeps them out of a pipeline's data). Levels from low to high: `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARNING`, `ERROR`, `CRITICAL`. `%(levelname)s`, `%(message)s`, `%(asctime)s` and `%(name)s` are the common format fields. Use `logging.getLogger(__name__)` in modules.

examples.code:
import logging, sys
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, level=logging.INFO, format='%(levelname)s %(message)s')
log = logging.getLogger('scan')
log.debug('hidden at INFO level')
log.info('scanning %s', '192.168.1.1')
log.warning('slow reply: %d ms', 420)
examples.out:
INFO scanning 192.168.1.1
WARNING slow reply: 420 ms

examples.desc: Logging goes to stderr, so the pipe carries only the data
examples.code: python3 -c 'import logging; logging.basicConfig(); logging.warning("slow reply"); print("data")' | wc -l

gotchas: Pass values as arguments (`log.info('x %s', value)`) rather than building the string yourself; formatting is skipped when the level is disabled.

blocks.name: argparse.ArgumentParser
blocks.sum: Define a command-line interface and parse sys.argv.

how.text: Declares positional arguments, options (`--top 5`), flags (`action='store_true'`) and types, then generates `--help` and error messages for free. `parse_args()` reads `sys.argv` and exits with status 2 on bad input. Passing an explicit list, `parse_args(['--top', '3'])`, makes the parser testable. [Modules and packaging](#py-modules) covers it in depth.

examples.code:
import argparse
p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog='loganalyzer')
p.add_argument('file', nargs='?', default='-')
p.add_argument('--top', type=int, default=5)
p.add_argument('--json', action='store_true')
args = p.parse_args(['--top', '3', 'access.log'])
print(args.file, args.top, args.json)

examples.desc: Feed option values to a parser from another command
examples.code: echo '--top 3' | xargs python3 -c 'import argparse; p = argparse.ArgumentParser(); p.add_argument("--top", type=int); print(p.parse_args().top)'

blocks.code:
import argparse
parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="loganalyzer", description="Summarize an access log.")
parser.add_argument("file", nargs="?", default="-", help="log file, or - for stdin")
parser.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=5)
parser.add_argument("--json", action="store_true")
print(parser.parse_args([]))
print(parser.parse_args(["--top", "10", "--json", "access.log"]))
parser.print_help()
blocks.out:
Namespace(file='-', top=5, json=False)
Namespace(file='access.log', top=10, json=True)

Summarize an access log.

positional arguments:
  file        log file, or - for stdin

options:

  --top TOP

blocks.text: In a real terminal, stdout and stderr are separate streams, and `2>/dev/null` hides the second. The in-page runner shows both together, so a program that writes errors to stderr looks as if it printed them normally. Test redirection behaviour in Terminal, not in the page.
Practice

blocks.title: Parse a log line

task.text: Write `parse(line)` that uses a regular expression to read one combined-format log line and returns a dict with `ip` (str), `method` (str), `path` (str), `status` (int) and `bytes` (int, with `-` counted as 0). Return `None` if the line does not match.

why.text: Named groups give each field a name, `match` anchors at the start, and `[^"]*` stops safely at the closing quote of the request. Converting to `int` once, at the parsing boundary, keeps the rest of the program free of string-to-number conversions.

ok = '198.51.100.8 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:15:40 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 5120 "-" "Googlebot/2.1"'
r = parse(ok)
assert r == {"ip": "198.51.100.8", "method": "GET", "path": "/index.html", "status": 200, "bytes": 5120}, r
dash = '10.0.0.1 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:15:40 +0000] "POST /login HTTP/1.1" 304 - "-" "x"'
assert parse(dash)["bytes"] == 0 and parse(dash)["method"] == "POST", parse(dash)
assert parse("garbage") is None
assert parse("") is None

task.text: Write `users_to_json(csv_text)` that takes the text of a CSV file with the header `name,role,ip,port` and returns a JSON string: a list of objects with `port` converted to an integer, with keys sorted (`sort_keys=True`) and no indentation.

blocks.title: Normalize timestamps

task.text: Write `to_utc(stamp)` that converts a log timestamp such as `07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 -0500` into an ISO 8601 string in UTC, for example `2026-10-07T14:14:08+00:00`.

why.text: `%z` makes the parsed datetime aware, `astimezone(timezone.utc)` shifts it (including the date rollover), and `isoformat()` writes an unambiguous string. Store and compare times in UTC; convert to local time only to display.

blocks.title: Real IPs only

task.text: Write `extract_ips(text)` that returns the list of valid IPv4 addresses found in free text, in order of appearance and without duplicates. Strings like `999.1.1.1` or `1.2.3` must not be returned.

why.text: The regex finds candidates by shape, `ipaddress.IPv4Address` rejects those with impossible octets, and the `found` list keeps first-seen order. A set would drop duplicates but lose the order.

blocks.title: A filter that reads stdin

task.text: Write a program that reads log lines from standard input and prints, for each status code, the number of lines that carry it, as `CODE COUNT` lines sorted by code. The status is the 9th whitespace-separated field. Skip blank lines. The sample input is provided as stdin.

blocks.solution:
import sys
from collections import Counter

counts = Counter(line.split()[8] for line in sys.stdin if line.strip())
for code in sorted(counts):
    print(code, counts[code])

why.text: Iterating `sys.stdin` gives lines lazily, `split()[8]` is `awk '{print $9}'` (fields are 0-based in Python), and `Counter` plus `sorted` replaces `sort | uniq -c`. The program uses no filename, so it works on a pipe or a redirected file.

blocks.title: Greedy trap

task.text: `quoted(text)` should return a list of the texts inside double quotes, but the greedy version below returns one wrong long match. Fix it.

why.text: `.*` is greedy and runs to the last quote on the line. The negated class `[^"]*` cannot cross a quote, so each match ends at the nearest closing quote. `.*?` would also work here.

questions.q: Why use `with open(...) as f:` instead of a bare `f = open(...)`?

options.text: It closes the file automatically, even if an error occurs inside the block
It lets you read and write at once
It converts the file to bytes

questions.why: `with` guarantees the file's `__exit__` runs, which flushes buffers and closes the descriptor on every path out of the block.

questions.q: What does `open("log.txt", "w")` do to an existing `log.txt`?

options.text: Truncates it to zero length immediately

questions.why: Mode `"w"` empties the file as soon as it is opened. Use `"a"` to append or `"x"` to fail when the file exists.

questions.q: Which regex part is the lazy form of `.*`?
questions.why: Adding `?` after a quantifier makes it match as little as possible.

options.text: `None`, because `match` only tries at the start of the string

questions.why: `match` is anchored at position 0. Use `re.search` to find the digits anywhere in the string.

questions.q: A script prints results with `print` and its error messages with `print(msg, file=sys.stderr)`. Why?

options.text: Pipes carry only stdout, so errors still reach the terminal without corrupting the data

questions.q: What does `subprocess.run(["ls", host], shell=False)` protect you from, compared with an f-string and `shell=True`?

options.text: Shell injection: special characters in `host` are never interpreted as commands

questions.why: With a list of arguments there is no shell to interpret `;`, `|` or `$()` in a value.

blocks.text: Step 1: The core, tested on a sample

`parse_line` applies the verbose named-group regex, `summarize` makes one pass over any iterable of lines (a file, `sys.stdin` or a `StringIO`), and `format_report` turns the result into text. Run it; the last line damages one record on purpose.

blocks.code:
import re
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from datetime import datetime

LOG_RE = re.compile(r"""
    ^(?P<ip>\S+)\s+\S+\s+\S+\s+            # client address, ident, user
    \[(?P<time>[^\]]+)\]\s+                 # [07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000]
    "(?P<method>[A-Z]+)\s+(?P<path>\S+)\s+[^"]*"\s+    # "GET /path HTTP/1.1"
    (?P<status>\d{3})\s+(?P<bytes>\d+|-)    # 200 5120
""", re.VERBOSE)
TIME_FMT = "%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z"


def parse_line(line):
    """Return a record dict for one log line, or None if it does not parse."""
    m = LOG_RE.match(line)
    if not m:
        return None
    rec = m.groupdict()
    rec["status"] = int(rec["status"])
    rec["bytes"] = 0 if rec["bytes"] == "-" else int(rec["bytes"])
    rec["time"] = datetime.strptime(rec["time"], TIME_FMT)
    return rec


def summarize(lines, top=5):
    """Read an iterable of lines in one pass and return a summary dict."""
    clients, codes, sent = Counter(), Counter(), defaultdict(int)
    minutes, missing = Counter(), Counter()
    total = bad = 0
    for line in lines:
        if not line.strip():
            continue
        rec = parse_line(line)
        if rec is None:
            bad += 1
            continue
        total += 1
        clients[rec["ip"]] += 1
        codes[rec["status"]] += 1
        sent[rec["ip"]] += rec["bytes"]
        minutes[rec["time"].strftime("%H:%M")] += 1
        if rec["status"] == 404:
            missing[rec["path"]] += 1
    by_bytes = sorted(sent.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))
    return {
        "requests": total,
        "unparsable": bad,
        "top_clients": clients.most_common(top),
        "status": dict(sorted(codes.items())),
        "bytes_per_client": by_bytes[:top],
        "busiest_minutes": minutes.most_common(top),
        "top_404_paths": missing.most_common(top),
    }


def format_report(s):
    """Turn a summary dict into a list of text lines."""
    out = [f"requests: {s['requests']}   unparsable: {s['unparsable']}", "", "top clients"]
    out += [f"  {ip:<16}{n:>5}" for ip, n in s["top_clients"]]
    out += ["", "status codes"]
    out += [f"  {code}  {n:>4}  {'#' * min(n, 40)}" for code, n in s["status"].items()]
    out += ["", "bytes per client"]
    out += [f"  {ip:<16}{n:>8}" for ip, n in s["bytes_per_client"]]
    out += ["", "busiest minutes"]
    out += [f"  {minute}  {n:>4}" for minute, n in s["busiest_minutes"]]
    out += ["", "most requested missing paths"]
    out += [f"  {n:>4}  {path}" for path, n in s["top_404_paths"]]
    return out

import io
SAMPLE = '''45.33.32.156 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000] "GET /api/v1/orders HTTP/1.1" 404 782 "-" "curl/8.4.0"
198.51.100.8 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:15 +0000] "GET /images/logo.png HTTP/1.1" 304 0 "-" "Googlebot/2.1"

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""loganalyzer.py - summarize a web-server access log (combined format).

Usage: loganalyzer.py [--top N] [--json] [FILE]
Reads FILE, or standard input when FILE is omitted or "-".
Exit status: 0 ok, 1 no valid lines, 2 file error.
"""
import argparse
import json
import signal
import sys
import re
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from datetime import datetime

LOG_RE = re.compile(r"""
    ^(?P<ip>\S+)\s+\S+\s+\S+\s+            # client address, ident, user
    \[(?P<time>[^\]]+)\]\s+                 # [07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000]
    "(?P<method>[A-Z]+)\s+(?P<path>\S+)\s+[^"]*"\s+    # "GET /path HTTP/1.1"
    (?P<status>\d{3})\s+(?P<bytes>\d+|-)    # 200 5120
""", re.VERBOSE)
TIME_FMT = "%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z"


def parse_line(line):
    """Return a record dict for one log line, or None if it does not parse."""
    m = LOG_RE.match(line)
    if not m:
        return None
    rec = m.groupdict()
    rec["status"] = int(rec["status"])
    rec["bytes"] = 0 if rec["bytes"] == "-" else int(rec["bytes"])
    rec["time"] = datetime.strptime(rec["time"], TIME_FMT)
    return rec


def summarize(lines, top=5):
    """Read an iterable of lines in one pass and return a summary dict."""
    clients, codes, sent = Counter(), Counter(), defaultdict(int)
    minutes, missing = Counter(), Counter()
    total = bad = 0
    for line in lines:
        if not line.strip():
            continue
        rec = parse_line(line)
        if rec is None:
            bad += 1
            continue
        total += 1
        clients[rec["ip"]] += 1
        codes[rec["status"]] += 1
        sent[rec["ip"]] += rec["bytes"]
        minutes[rec["time"].strftime("%H:%M")] += 1
        if rec["status"] == 404:
            missing[rec["path"]] += 1
    by_bytes = sorted(sent.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))
    return {
        "requests": total,
        "unparsable": bad,
        "top_clients": clients.most_common(top),
        "status": dict(sorted(codes.items())),
        "bytes_per_client": by_bytes[:top],
        "busiest_minutes": minutes.most_common(top),
        "top_404_paths": missing.most_common(top),
    }


def format_report(s):
    """Turn a summary dict into a list of text lines."""
    out = [f"requests: {s['requests']}   unparsable: {s['unparsable']}", "", "top clients"]
    out += [f"  {ip:<16}{n:>5}" for ip, n in s["top_clients"]]
    out += ["", "status codes"]
    out += [f"  {code}  {n:>4}  {'#' * min(n, 40)}" for code, n in s["status"].items()]
    out += ["", "bytes per client"]
    out += [f"  {ip:<16}{n:>8}" for ip, n in s["bytes_per_client"]]
    out += ["", "busiest minutes"]
    out += [f"  {minute}  {n:>4}" for minute, n in s["busiest_minutes"]]
    out += ["", "most requested missing paths"]
    out += [f"  {n:>4}  {path}" for path, n in s["top_404_paths"]]
    return out


def main(argv=None, stdin=None):
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Summarize a web-server access log.")
    parser.add_argument("file", nargs="?", default="-", help="log file, or - for standard input")
    parser.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=5, help="how many rows per table (default 5)")
    parser.add_argument("--json", action="store_true", help="print JSON instead of text")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    try:
        if args.file == "-":
            summary = summarize(stdin if stdin is not None else sys.stdin, args.top)
        else:
            with open(args.file, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
                summary = summarize(f, args.top)
    except OSError as err:
        print(f"loganalyzer: {err}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    if args.json:
        print(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))
    else:
        print("\n".join(format_report(summary)))
    return 0 if summary["requests"] else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if hasattr(signal, "SIGPIPE"):
        signal.signal(signal.SIGPIPE, signal.SIG_DFL)   # quiet exit when piped into head
    sys.exit(main())

A string prefixed with r in which backslashes are kept literally; the right form for regex patterns
A quantifier that matches as much text as possible before giving back
Parentheses in a regex that remember the text they matched

The number a program returns to the shell: 0 for success, non-zero for failure
